article.title: Send a message with the API
article.excerpt: One endpoint accepts asynchronously. A success code means the platform took the message — not that a handset received it.

p: Endpoint and headers below. All request and response bodies are UTF-8 JSON.

sections.note: The platform sends the content you give it. It does not render template variables for you, and template definitions live in your provider account, not here.

sections.h: Start with TRANSACTIONAL, not with the default
p: messageType is the only input to the suppression gate. The platform does not read your message body — so an alert that happens to contain promotional wording will pass as TRANSACTIONAL even though, under rules like the US TCPA, it may still be legally marketing. Declaring the type honestly is the caller's responsibility.

An unrecognised value is rejected with HTTP 400 and code 40000 rather than silently downgraded. That is deliberate: a typo should surface as a broken integration, not as verification codes that quietly stop arriving.
sections.scope: Suppression applies to marketing traffic only, and opt-out handling is an SMS concept here. Email and WhatsApp connect on the same model, but they do not carry this suppression gate today.

p: The response repeats the recipient, names the provider that actually carried the message, and returns the fields you will want at reconciliation time.

sections.h: The one rule that prevents most duplicate sends
p: There is no idempotency key. Sending the same request twice sends two messages and bills for two. Because acceptance is asynchronous, a network timeout means the send may already have happened — treat the timeout as unknown, not as failure.
list: Got a messageId: query its status or wait for the callback. Do not resend.
Did not get a messageId: look the send up in the console log by time window and recipient number. Do not resend.
A client-side timeout never rolls back a message that was already submitted.
